summary: RELOAD has no generic service discovery mechanism in its base protocol, RFC 6940. This document defines how the Recursive Distributed Rendezvous mechanism, ReDiR, can be used in RELOAD overlays to find services.

eli5.summary: In a big club with no front desk, how do you find who offers a service? This RFC sets up a simple way for members to register and look up services.

questions: how does reload service discovery work
subtitle: How peers in a RELOAD overlay find who offers a service, using a tree of lookups called ReDiR.

tldr.problem: The RELOAD base protocol has no generic service discovery, and storing every provider under one well-known key overloads whichever node holds that key.
tldr.mechanism: Providers of each service register in a tree stored in the overlay with ordinary Store and Fetch requests. A seeker walks the tree up or down until it finds the provider whose Node-ID follows its own.
tldr.outcome: RELOAD gets a generic service discovery mechanism without any change to the base protocol, backed by a new access control policy, a new Kind and new IANA registries.

today: RFC 7374 is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It builds on the RELOAD base protocol, RFC 6940.

sections.title: The Service Discovery Problem
sections.content:
RELOAD (RFC 6940) is a peer-to-peer signaling protocol that maintains an overlay network and stores and retrieves data in it. It defines service discovery only for TURN, not generically. Example services that peers might offer include a TURN relay, a voice mail service, a gateway location service and a transcoding service.

The naive approach stores the Node-IDs of all providers under one well-known key. That scales linearly with the number of providers, and the node responsible for the key may be overloaded because all lookups for that service land on it. The RFC says this simple approach may suit a very small overlay of perhaps tens of nodes.

This document applies Recursive Distributed Rendezvous (ReDiR) to RELOAD. It is aimed at overlays where tens of thousands of nodes or more may make lookups and where around one in ten peers may offer the service.
sections.eli5: If one person keeps the list of every helper, that person gets swamped with questions. ReDiR spreads the list around so nobody gets swamped.

sections.title: How the ReDiR Tree Works
sections.content:
ReDiR needs nothing new from RELOAD. It builds a tree of the providers of one service and stores it in the overlay using Store and Fetch requests. Each service is named by a namespace, a UTF-8 string such as voice-mail or turn-server, and each namespace has its own tree.

The root is at level 0, its children at level 1, and so on. The tree has a branching factor b, so level lvl has room for at most b to the power lvl nodes. A node is identified by a pair (lvl,j), where j is its position from the left. Each node holds a dictionary of provider entries and covers b intervals of the identifier space. A node is stored under the key H(namespace,level,j), so the root for voice mail is at H("voice-mail",0,0).

A lookup for identifier k returns the provider in that namespace whose Node-ID is the closest successor of k. Lookups need a logarithmic number of Fetches, and typically a constant number if the starting level is chosen well and Node-IDs are uniformly random. In a real tree the default branching factor is 10 and the identifier space is at least 2^128.
sections.eli5: Think of a family tree of piles of cards. The top pile covers everyone, and each level down splits the club into smaller groups, so you can zoom in on your neighborhood quickly.

sections.title: The RedirServiceProvider Record
sections.content:
Tree nodes use the dictionary data model of RELOAD, and the dictionary key is the Node-ID of the provider. The value is a RedirServiceProvider resource record containing:

  • type: the type of an optional extension; unknown types are allowed.
  • destination_list: the IDs through which a message is routed to reach the provider.
  • namespace: the UTF-8 namespace string.
  • level and node: where in the tree the record is stored.
  • length: the length of the rest of the record.

The record can be extended with information about the service or provider.

The REDIR Kind is named by concatenating namespace, level and node number. Its Kind-ID is 0x104, assigned by IANA.
sections.eli5: Each card says who the helper is, how to reach them, which club service they offer, and which pile the card belongs in.

sections.title: Registering, Refreshing and Looking Up
sections.content:
Both registration and lookup start at a level Lstart. The RFC RECOMMENDS 2. As an optimization a node MAY reuse the lowest level where its last registration finished, or take the mode of the levels where its last 16 lookups completed.

Registration. A node MUST do a wildcard Fetch and then a Store of its record in the tree node responsible for the interval enclosing its Node-ID at the starting level. If its Node-ID is the lowest or highest in that interval it MUST keep going up toward the root, repeating both steps at each level. It MUST also walk down from Lstart, storing its record wherever it is the lowest or highest in its interval, and stop when it is the only provider in its interval.

Refresh. All ReDiR state is soft. Providers MUST repeat the whole registration periodically until they leave, and expired records MUST be dropped. A default lifetime of 10 minutes is RECOMMENDED, and a refresh SHOULD start slightly early, for example at 90% of the interval. Before leaving, a provider SHOULD remove its records by storing exists=False.

Lookup. The seeker fetches the node at the current level and then applies three conditions. (1) If no successor is in the fetched node, go up one level. (2) If its ID is neither the lowest nor the highest in its interval, go down one level. (3) Otherwise the successor found is the answer. If the walk reaches the root with no successor, an appropriate strategy is to pick a root entry at random. A node MAY also keep a temporary cache of entries seen during the lookup to recover from rare failures when a record expires just before its refresh arrives.
sections.eli5: To sign up, you put your card in the pile for your neighborhood and in bigger piles above it if you are first or last in line. To find a helper, you check piles, going up when yours is empty and down when it is crowded, until the next helper after you turns up.

sections.title: A Four-Provider Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a tiny overlay with numBitsInNodeId=4 (16 identifiers) and branching factor 2. Providers with Node-IDs 2, 3, 7 and 4 register one after another, all starting at level 2. Peer 2 finds the tree empty, so it climbs all the way to the root. Peer 3 climbs too because it is the highest in its interval. Peer 7 is alone in its interval at level 1, and peer 4 is the lowest in its interval at level 2, so both also reach the root.

Peer 5 then looks up a provider. At level 2 it fetches the second node from the left, sees a successor (peer 7) and finds that 5 is the highest in its interval, so the lookup finishes at once with peer 7. If peer 5 started at level 3 instead, it would fetch an empty node, move up to level 2 and reach the same answer.
sections.eli5: Four helpers sign up, and a kid numbered 5 asks for help. After checking one pile, the kid learns that helper number 7 is the next one up, and goes to them.

sections.title: Access Control, Configuration and Security
sections.content:
None of the access control policies in RELOAD fit ReDiR, so this RFC defines NODE-ID-MATCH. A value MUST be written only if the request is signed with a key whose certificate Node-ID equals the dictionary key. When exists=True, the Node-ID MUST fall in one of the node's intervals, and H(namespace,level,node) MUST equal the Resource-ID. It may be used only with dictionary types.

The security section explains the effect: only a provider can store a pointer to itself, which prevents a malicious node from inserting pointers to others, and a node can store only one record per level, which prevents flooding the tree with entries. Attacks such as refusing to store a value are covered by RELOAD itself.

The overlay configuration document gets a new branching-factor element under the REDIR kind, with default 10, in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:p2p:redir.

IANA registered the NODE-ID-MATCH policy, the XML namespace URI, Kind-ID 0x104 and a new "RELOAD Services Registry" (Specification Required) whose initial entries are turn-server and voice-mail. For TURN server discovery, ReDiR can serve as an alternative to the mechanism in the base specification.
sections.eli5: Only the helper may write their own card, and only in the right pile, so nobody can stuff the piles with fake cards.
